1: Shows personal and professional values and behaviour in line with Good Medical Practice.
Communicates clearly with patients, families and the wider team, including being open when things go wrong.
Uses strong interpersonal skills, showing empathy, compassion, courtesy and respect.
Recognises how their own conduct affects patients and colleagues, and adjusts it.
Reflects on their own practice to gain insight and learn from experience.
Obtains valid consent in line with legal and professional principles.
Takes part in the GMC National Training Survey and other quality assurance processes.
Keeps accurate, legible, timely notes for all clinical practice.
Values physical and mental health, both their own and others'.
2: Advises less experienced colleagues on professional issues.
Plans care for complex patients, knows their limits and asks for help.
Understands how behaviour affects care quality and patient safety.
Sets a positive example for juniors and the wider team.
Stays professional and situationally aware in emergencies.
Breaks bad news sensitively, considering cultural and social differences.
Recognises how work patterns and lifestyle affect health, and acts to reduce the impact.
3: Takes charge of problems that arise during patient care.
Plans care for complex patients, even outside guidelines, and asks for help when needed.
Engages in appraisal and explains job planning, performance management and revalidation.
Follows governance rules and encourages the team to do the same.
Supports wellbeing, spots struggling colleagues and escalates when needed.
Applies equality and diversity law in everyday work.

1: Knows how the anaesthetic department is run and how it fits within the hospital.
Understands employment law and why working time rules matter.
Works within local and national clinical governance and data protection systems.
Keeps up to date with, and follows, GMC and other professional guidance.
Supports the aims of the hospital as an organisation.
Applies health and safety law to patient care.
2: Helps run anaesthetic services within hospital management and links them to regional specialist services.
Applies legal and ethical principles, especially around consent and shared decisions.
Works with departmental systems that deliver perioperative care.
Uses digital systems competently in patient care.
3: Explains how trust or health board management structures work together.
Outlines how the NHS and wider health and social care are organised.
Explains how national health policy is made, implemented and monitored.
Understands and encourages the roles of different health professionals.
Describes workforce planning methods and their limits.
Uses management and teamwork skills in complex, fast-changing situations.
Describes how healthcare is commissioned and funded.
Knows how to write medicolegal statements and work with agencies on legal duties.
Follows rules on information governance, data protection and records.
Carries out departmental management and administrative tasks.
Meets contractual obligations and takes part in appraisal.

1: Takes an active part in team tasks and helps the team succeed.
Behaves in a way that shows suitable clinical leadership.
Shows why non-technical skills such as communication and teamwork matter.
Describes what leaders are responsible for.
Explains why good leadership is key to safe, effective care.
Gives, receives and uses helpful feedback.
2: Supports and guides less experienced colleagues.
Understands their own leadership style and its effect on others.
Reviews their decisions critically and explains their reasoning.
Encourages and works well in multiprofessional teams.
Uses teamwork skills in complex, fast-changing situations.
3: Shows clinical leadership in a special interest area.
Leads the multidisciplinary team in planning complex care.
Works effectively with the whole theatre and perioperative team.
Keeps strong situational awareness of self and team.
Gathers and shares information, anticipating problems.
Reviews the performance of colleagues and systems to drive best practice.
Leads in a way that supports and engages the team.
Promotes openness, supports colleagues and respects differing views.
Adapts leadership style to improve engagement and outcomes.
Addresses difficult team behaviour and escalates when needed.
Describes their role in a major incident.

1: Explains quality improvement theories and methods.

Identifies common threats to patient safety in theatre and how routine practice reduces them.
Values shared learning through incident reporting and morbidity and mortality reviews.

Understands non-technical skills: situation awareness, task management, decision-making and teamwork.
Understands structured communication and cognitive aids in emergencies, and the role of simulation.
Knows the benefits and limits of technology and equipment for patient safety.
Explains and demonstrates the duty of candour.
2: Knows when and how to use QI methods without compromising safety.
Recognises the factors that affect reliable care.
Tells expected variation from unwarranted variation.
Uses suitable measures to show whether a change has improved care.
Knows the difference between data for assurance and data for improvement.
Uses simple proactive techniques to prevent harm, judging likelihood and severity.
Matches expertise and resources to the clinical risk.
Explains how anaesthetists' actions affect safety across the system.
Describes the principles of medication safety.
Explains how critical incidents are followed up.
3: Leads a local QI project in a special interest area, tracking outcomes that matter to patients.
Explains how complexity theory applies to healthcare.
Identifies the levers and psychology of managing change.
Identifies and engages people affected by change.
Combines psychological, system and technical knowledge to deliver change.

Evaluates whether a QI intervention worked.

1: Keeps patient care the priority in educational settings.
Plans and runs their own learning.
Takes part in welcoming and orienting new staff.

1: Keeps up with guidelines and key publications using unbiased literature searches.
Explains the principles of Good Clinical Practice.
Explains how research evidence shapes clinical decisions.
Describes the main statistical techniques used in research.
2: Judges the quality of research and its place in the literature before changing practice.
